A 77-year-old male with a 30+ year history of poorly managed type 2 diabetes (with complications
including retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy) and coronary artery disease seeks medical
attention. He reports losing 7 kg over three months and experiences early satiety with epigastric
discomfort. He has post-prandial nausea and vomiting that improves with fasting, but no changes in
bowel movements. His treatment includes insulin glargine nightly and insulin aspart before meals. His

HbA1c is 9.2% (normal range: 4.3-5.6%). Physical examination reveals a weight of 87 kg, BMI of 29,
mild epigastric tenderness, and no scleral icterus. The remainder of the examination is normal. What is
the most appropriate first diagnostic test for this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Abdominal ultrasound
(B) Capsule endoscopy (C) Gastric manometry (D) Hydrogen breath test (E)
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (F) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (G) Scintigraphic
gastric-emptying study (H) Fecal occult blood test (I) Hydrogen breath test for small intestinal bacterial
overgrowth (J) Serum gastrin level measurement
 A. Scintigraphic gastric-emptying study
B. Serum gastrin level measurement
C. Fecal occult blood test
D. Abdominal ultrasound
E. Capsule endoscopy
F. Gastric manometry
G. Hydrogen breath test
H. Hydrogen breath test for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
I. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy
J. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
